tips.title: Turn off automatic renewals and renew only what you still use
tips.cost: No cost. Review Google Play subscriptions, Apple subscriptions, UPI Autopay, and your card's standing instructions. Cancel through the same channel that holds the mandate.
tips.inPlainWords: You save exactly the subscriptions you no longer use but are still paying for. Spend 20 minutes reviewing the auto-pay and mandate lists in Google Play, the App Store, your UPI app and your card statements. In India, an e-mandate for a recurring card or UPI payment must be registered with a pre-debit notification, and you can cancel it through your bank or the app.
tips.benefit: The saving is the total of the subscriptions you no longer need; there is no single figure. The RBI's e-mandate rules require a pre-debit notification before a recurring card or UPI payment, and the bank or app must let you cancel the mandate. A merchant cannot force a renewal after cancellation. A annual plan is often cheaper than a monthly one for a service you actually use.
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India, e-mandate framework. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; National Payments Corporation of India, UPI Autopay. <https://www.npci.org.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: Turning off auto-renew can lose a promotional price. Keep the annual plan for a service you use weekly; cancel the rest. Check the card statement for a merchant you do not recognise.

tips.title: File your income-tax return every year, and claim every deduction you are allowed
tips.cost: Free on the Income Tax Department's e-filing portal. A tax preparer or chartered accountant charges a fee; for a simple salary return you do not need one.
tips.inPlainWords: You often get money back. Tax is deducted at source from salary, bank interest and other income on the basis of what you declared, and the deduction is only an estimate: if you did not claim house-rent allowance, the deduction for home-loan interest, or a health-insurance premium, the return is where you claim it. Check Form 26AS and the Annual Information Statement on the e-filing portal, choose the return form that matches your income, and file before the due date, which is normally 31 July and is sometimes extended. If your income is below the basic exemption limit and no refund is due, you usually need not file, but check the other triggers first.
tips.benefit: The return settles the tax for the year: excess tax deducted at source is refunded to your bank account and a shortfall is paid. It is also the document banks, lenders and visa officers ask for, and it is how you carry a capital loss forward. In India the choice between the old regime and the new regime changes which deductions you get, so compute both and pick the one that costs less. A mistake can be corrected with a revised return, and a missed year can sometimes be covered by an updated return on payment of additional tax.
tips.sources: Income Tax Department, e-filing portal. <https://www.incometax.gov.in/>; Income-tax Act, 1961. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Central Board of Direct Taxes. <https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Filing late costs a fee and interest, and a wrong claim can be reopened. Keep the proofs — rent receipts, the insurance premium receipt, the home-loan interest certificate — because the department's pre-filled data and your own records often disagree. Most deductions you claim under the old regime are not available under the new one, so the cheaper regime is not always the one with more deductions. A refund is not a windfall: it is your own money that was withheld during the year.

tips.title: Your EPF is not only for buying a home: it can also pay rent, a housing loan, medical bills and some life events
tips.cost: No fee on the EPFO portal. A bank or employer may ask for documents. An agent who charges a commission is not necessary.
tips.inPlainWords: The Employees' Provident Fund is not limited to a home purchase. EPFO rules allow a member to withdraw or advance funds for buying or building a house, repaying a housing loan, paying rent in some cases, treatment of a serious illness, marriage or education, and a few other purposes. The amount and the conditions depend on the purpose and the number of years of service. Apply through the EPFO member portal, not an agent.
tips.benefit: The EPF Scheme, 1952 and the EPFO's circulars set the withdrawal and advance categories. A member can take an advance for a house purchase or construction, for repayment of a housing loan, for rent in specified cases, for illness, for marriage or education, and for a few other needs. The account earns interest declared annually by the EPFO. On death, the nominee or legal heir can withdraw the balance. An early withdrawal reduces the retirement corpus.
tips.sources: Employees' Provident Fund Organisation, member portal. <https://www.epfo.gov.in/>; Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952. <https://labour.gov.in/>; Income-tax Department, EPF taxation. <https://www.incometax.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The purpose and the eligible amount change with the EPFO circulars. A withdrawal for a non-eligible purpose can be rejected and may attract tax. Check the passbook and the UAN before applying.

tips.title: Review your mobile and broadband plans once a year, and escalate a refused downgrade instead of accepting it
tips.cost: No cost. It takes a few minutes with the operator's app and your last six bills. The real effort is holding your ground when the call centre offers an upgrade instead.
tips.inPlainWords: A plan you took two years ago often costs more than the plan on sale today for the same data. Work out your real monthly usage from the operator's app or your bills, then ask for the cheaper plan that matches it. If the operator refuses, delays the change or says only a store visit can do it, ask for that in writing and escalate. In India the route is the operator's customer care, then its nodal officer and appellate authority, then the regulator or a consumer forum. Number portability is a separate right: you can move to another operator and keep your number.
tips.benefit: The saving is the gap between your old monthly rent and the current plan, multiplied by twelve, plus the add-ons you no longer need. Indian operators must publish their tariffs, and a change of plan or a porting request has to be handled within the timelines the regulator sets. The Telecom Consumers Complaint Redressal Regulations give every operator a three-level grievance route — call centre, nodal officer and appellate authority — and require a complaint reference number, so an oral 'no' is not the end of the matter. If the operator still refuses, the National Consumer Helpline and a consumer commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 are open to you.
tips.sources: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India. <https://trai.gov.in/>; Department of Telecommunications. <https://dot.gov.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A 'free' upgrade often resets a lock-in or bundles a service you start paying for after a few months. Check whether the cheaper plan keeps the data, the speed and the add-ons you use, and whether your broadband has a fair-usage cap that slows you after a limit. Porting does not cancel dues; clear the outstanding bill first. Keep the complaint number — without it, an escalation has no date to work from.

tips.title: Do not buy lottery tickets as an investment
tips.cost: Nothing. Not buying is the saving. If you play, set a fixed entertainment amount and treat it as already spent.
tips.inPlainWords: A lottery is a negative-sum game: the operator keeps a share of every rupee for prizes, administration and the state, so the average ticket returns less than it costs. Exactly how much is returned depends on the scheme and on the state that runs it, and the rules are published, but the direction never changes. In India lotteries are a state subject: the Lotteries (Regulation) Act, 1998 lets a state organise, restrict or ban them, and many states have banned paper lotteries. A ticket is entertainment, not saving.
tips.benefit: The arithmetic is the argument. Whatever the payout share, the money not returned is the operator's, the state's and the retailer's, so the expected value of a ticket is below its price and repeated play converges on that loss. No skill, system or lucky number changes a draw. India also taxes the win: a prize above the threshold is taxed at the flat rate for lottery income, and the seller deducts it at source, so the amount received is smaller than the advertised prize. The reliable return comes from the money you do not spend.
tips.sources: Lotteries (Regulation) Act, 1998. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Portal of India. <https://www.india.gov.in/>; Income Tax Department. <https://www.incometax.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Anyone selling a 'system' or a guaranteed win is a scam; a state draw has no pattern to beat. Online lotteries are prohibited under the 1998 Act, and the online gaming law of 2025 bans real-money games, so an offshore app is neither a legal route nor a forum that will pay you. If gambling is taking money you need, treat it as a health problem rather than a budgeting one and talk to someone. Keep any entertainment money separate from savings, and never borrow to play.

tips.title: Walk away from 'guaranteed returns' and 'sure profit' offers
tips.cost: No cost to check. Search the SEBI and RBI websites, and ask for the scheme's registration number in writing.
tips.inPlainWords: No legitimate investment in India guarantees a return or protects the principal. SEBI and the RBI require risk disclosures, and a scheme that promises a fixed high return is either unauthorised or a fraud. If the offer is urgent, secret or paid to a personal account, it is a scam. Check the entity on the SEBI and RBI registries before you send money.
tips.benefit: SEBI's investor charter and the RBI's rules prohibit misleading claims and unauthorised deposit-taking. A collective investment scheme needs SEBI registration, and a deposit-taking entity needs RBI authorisation. The BNS, 2023 punishes cheating, and the Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act, 2019 punishes unregulated deposit schemes. A promise of a high fixed return is a warning sign, not a feature.
tips.sources: Securities and Exchange Board of India, investor education. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, unauthorised entities. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: Past returns do not guarantee future returns. A 'fixed return' insurance plan is not a bank deposit. A friend or relative who sells the scheme may be a victim too.

tips.title: Avoid making minimum payments or taking installment plans or consumer loans
tips.cost: No cost at all. You must keep enough cash on hand to pay the full balance by the due date. The hard part is resisting the urge to spread out large purchases via installment plans.
tips.inPlainWords: Making minimum payments is not a discount — it is essentially a daily‑interest loan that works out to roughly 18% per year. Once you use this option, the interest‑free period ends immediately, and the unpaid portion of the balance accrues interest from that point onward. Always look at the annual percentage rate when comparing offers; regulators now require issuers to display this figure prominently, rather than just the daily rate. The minimum rate is exactly 0.7 times the maximum rate.
tips.benefit: Before 2020, credit‑card interest rates were capped: the maximum daily rate was 0.05% and the minimum was 70% of that cap. At 0.05% daily, the annual simple interest rate comes to 18.25%. Starting in 2021, issuers and cardholders can negotiate rates freely. After opting for minimum payments, the unpaid balance continues to accrue interest daily while the interest‑free period is lost.
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India, credit cards and loans. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: The 18.25% figure results from multiplying 0.05% by 365 without compounding; the actual rate would be higher if interest were compounded monthly. Some banks offer discounts, but you must refer to the annual rate listed on your own statement. If you truly cannot afford the payment, seek a lower‑rate loan from a reputable lender rather than letting minimum payments pile up.

tips.title: Turn off one-tap payments before you tip a streamer or buy inside a game
tips.cost: No cost. A few minutes to remove the saved card, cancel the UPI Autopay mandate and set a spend limit in the app store.
tips.inPlainWords: A tip to a streamer and an in-game purchase are ordinary payments: once made, the money is the platform's and there is no general right to a refund because you regretted it. The protection is preventive. Remove the saved card from the streaming and gaming apps, cancel the recurring mandate in your UPI app or with the bank, and switch on the app store's spend limit or its 'ask before buying' setting. An adult who taps pay has consented. A child who taps pay has not, because a minor's contract is void in India, so the guardian can demand the money back.
tips.benefit: The saving is the sum of small taps that never feel like spending — a top-up, a skin, a gift — and it is usually invisible until the statement arrives. The mechanics that make it easy are exactly the ones you can switch off: stored cards, one-click checkout, auto-debit mandates, and in-game currencies that hide the rupee price. India's e-mandate rules require a pre-debit notification before a recurring card or UPI payment, which gives you a warning and a cancellation route. If a minor made the purchase, the platform's refund policy and the law on minors' contracts both support the guardian's claim.
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India, e-mandates. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: An app store refund is a goodwill policy, not a right, and it is usually one-time. A card chargeback is for an unauthorised or undelivered payment, not for buyer's remorse. Put a child's account under a family setting that requires approval for purchases, and read the statement every month, because the small amounts are the ones that escape notice. The 2025 ban on real-money online games does not make an in-game purchase refundable.

tips.title: A child's large in-app purchase can be reversed: a minor's contract is void, and the guardian can ask for a refund
tips.cost: No cost to file a platform complaint. A consumer complaint has a small fee. A lawyer's fee if the amount is large and the platform refuses.
tips.inPlainWords: In India, a person under 18 is a minor, and an agreement with a minor is void under section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. A large in-app purchase or gift made by a child without the guardian's consent can be challenged, and the platform or the app store can be asked to reverse it. The practical route is the platform's refund process, then the consumer commission if it refuses.
tips.benefit: Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 makes an agreement by a minor void, and the guardian can seek restitution of the money. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers a deficient service and an unfair trade practice, and the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 require a grievance officer. The RBI's card and UPI chargeback rules may help if the payment was unauthorised. The platform's own parental-control and refund policy is the first step.
tips.sources: Indian Contract Act, 1872 (section 11). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, chargebacks. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>
tips.caveats: Proving the child made the purchase is the hard part; keep the device logs, the timestamps and the child's statement. A parent who knowingly allowed the purchase may not get a refund. Set a spending limit and do not share the payment PIN.

tips.title: Teach the child one rule: anyone who asks for a parent's phone, OTP or UPI PIN is a scammer
tips.cost: No cost. Set a UPI limit, enable parental controls and keep the payment PIN to yourself.
tips.inPlainWords: The scams change, but the last step is always the same: the child is asked to use a parent's phone, read out an OTP or approve a UPI request. Teach the child that no teacher, police officer, game moderator or 'customer care' agent needs the parent's phone or OTP. Add: 'If something goes wrong, tell me at once; I will not shout at you.' A child who is afraid to speak up loses more money.
tips.benefit: The RBI and the cyber crime police state that no bank, police officer or government agency asks for an OTP, PIN or password. The BNS, 2023 and the IT Act, 2000 punish cheating and identity theft. The 1930 helpline and cybercrime.gov.in can freeze a fraudulent transfer if it is reported quickly. A family code word and a spending limit on the child's own account reduce the risk.
tips.sources: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, awareness. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A caller can spoof a number and use a fake logo. A video call is not proof. Do not scold the child before you have reported the fraud; the report matters more.

tips.title: Skipping extended warranties for electronics
tips.cost: There’s no upfront cost. The trade‑off is that after the warranty expires you’ll have to pay for any repairs yourself — though that scenario is relatively unlikely.
tips.inPlainWords: Extended warranties typically cost 10% to 50% of the item’s original price. The profit margin on these warranties is roughly ten times higher than that of regular merchandise. In 2003, Best Buy in the U.S. earned over half of its total profits from extended warranties, even though they accounted for only 3% to 4% of its overall revenue. That price gap is exactly the extra money you end up paying.
tips.benefit: Extended warranties are priced at 10% to 50% of the product’s original cost. Industry estimates cited in research show that the average gross margin on these warranties sits at 50% to 60%: for every 100 dollars spent on a warranty, 50 to 60 dollars become pure profit. This is roughly 18 times higher than the gross margin on ordinary goods. In 2003, extended warranties made up just 3% to 4% of Best Buy’s revenue yet generated over 50% of its total profits (U.S. retail data from the early 2000s).
tips.sources: Chen T, Kalra A, Sun B (2009). Why Do Consumers Buy Extended Service Contracts? Journal of Consumer Research 36(4):611-623. <https://doi.org/10.1086/605298>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Bureau of Indian Standards. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The gross‑margin figure comes from an industry estimate referenced in the paper (Business Week, 2004); it wasn’t measured directly by the authors. The calculations above apply to ordinary consumers who can afford a single repair bill. For people who rely on a single device and lack a backup, the calculation changes. Screen‑protection plans for phones must also be evaluated separately: first estimate how often you’re likely to drop the phone, then decide whether the premium is worth it.

tips.title: Ask for the generic by its salt name, and check the Jan Aushadhi price and the NPPA ceiling before you pay
tips.cost: No cost. You ask the doctor for the salt name and the pharmacist for the generic version, and you can look up the ceiling price and the Jan Aushadhi price for free.
tips.inPlainWords: A brand name is a manufacturer's label; the medicine is the salt — paracetamol, metformin, amoxicillin. Ask the doctor to write the salt name, then ask the pharmacy whether it stocks a generic of the same strength. There is no separate 'consistency evaluation' category in India: a generic is approved by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, or by a state drug controller for some products, on the basis of the same active ingredient and, where required, bioequivalence data. Prices of scheduled formulations are capped by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority, and Jan Aushadhi Kendras sell generics at prices below the market.
tips.benefit: The same active ingredient at the same dose usually costs a fraction of the branded price, and the gap is widest for long-term medicines — diabetes, blood pressure, thyroid, cholesterol — where the bill repeats every month. Two official checks make the choice concrete: the NPPA ceiling price tells you the most a scheduled formulation may be sold for, and the Jan Aushadhi price list tells you what a government-supported generic costs. A generic outside the ceiling list can still be far cheaper than the brand. For a chronic medicine the annual saving can cover the monitoring tests that matter more than the brand.
tips.sources: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/>; National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority. <https://www.nppaindia.nic.in/>; Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Bureau of India, Jan Aushadhi. <https://janaushadhi.gov.in/>; Department of Pharmaceuticals. <https://pharmaceuticals.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A generic must contain the same active ingredient, but the fillers, the coating and the manufacturer can differ, and quality failures do occur — the drug regulator publishes lists of batches that fail testing. Buy from a licensed pharmacy with a visible drug licence, check the batch number and the expiry, and keep the bill. If you switch a chronic medicine, measure the result — blood pressure, HbA1c, thyroid function — instead of relying on how you feel, and tell the doctor if it changes. Never stop a medicine on your own. Original brands remain available at a higher price.

tips.title: India has no 'family sharing' of an individual medical account; use PM-JAY, ESIC or a state scheme for the household
tips.cost: PM-JAY is free for eligible households. ESIC and CGHS are contribution or subscription based. A private insurance policy is separate.
tips.inPlainWords: India does not have the individual medical-savings account that some countries allow a family to share. The Indian route is a household scheme: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY for eligible families, ESIC for covered employees, CGHS for central government staff, and a state health scheme. Check who is covered and what the empanelment is. Do not pay a private agent to 'link' a family.
tips.benefit: PM-JAY provides hospital cover for eligible households through empanelled hospitals, with the cover shared by the family. ESIC covers insured workers and their dependants for specified treatment. CGHS covers central government employees and pensioners. State schemes vary. The National Health Authority runs PM-JAY, and the eligibility is based on the SECC and state lists. A household should check the Ayushman card and the empanelled hospital list before an emergency.
tips.sources: National Health Authority, Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>; Employees' State Insurance Corporation. <https://esic.gov.in/>; Central Government Health Scheme. <https://cghs.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Coverage is for listed procedures and empanelled hospitals; not every cost is covered. A 'family card' sold by an agent is not a government scheme. Check the NHA and state health department websites.

tips.title: Drink filtered water from a reusable bottle instead of buying bottled water, but do not assume the tap is safe
tips.cost: A purifier and a steel bottle cost money once; boiling costs a little gas or electricity. Bottled water costs tens of rupees a litre, every day.
tips.inPlainWords: The saving is real: municipal water costs a fraction of a rupee a litre, bottled water costs tens of rupees, and the gap compounds over a year. But the instruction to 'just boil the tap water' does not transfer to India. Boiling kills bacteria and viruses; it does not remove lead, arsenic, nitrate, pesticides or the taste of a contaminated supply, and many Indian cities do not deliver water that is drinkable at the tap without treatment. Use a purifier matched to the local water — reverse osmosis where the dissolved solids are high, ultraviolet or a good filter where they are not — and get the water tested if several people in the building fall ill.
tips.benefit: A household that moves from bottled water to a purifier and a reusable bottle usually recovers the cost of the purifier within months, and stops carrying plastic. The health side matters as much: a purifier serviced on schedule and a bottle washed daily are more dependable than an unregulated 'mineral water' can. Packaged drinking water sold in India must carry the ISI mark under the Indian Standard for packaged drinking water and an FSSAI licence number, so you can judge what you are buying by the label rather than the brand. Water is also the cheapest line in the household budget to fix, which is why the saving is worth the setup.
tips.sources: Ministry of Jal Shakti, drinking water. <https://jalshakti-ddws.gov.in/>; Bureau of Indian Standards. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. <https://mohua.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Boiling is not purification: it concentrates whatever is dissolved in the water. A filter that is not replaced becomes a bacterial growth medium, so follow the service interval. A building's tank and pipes can undo a good municipal supply, which is why a change in taste or colour is worth reporting. If the supply is contaminated, complain to the municipal corporation or the state water authority and stop drinking it; a home filter is not a substitute for a clean source. Bottled water is worth the money when you are travelling or when the supply has failed, not as a year-round default.

tips.title: Infrequent stock trading
tips.cost: There are no monetary costs. The real challenge is resisting the urge to trade whenever you see market news.
tips.inPlainWords: Among investors who trade most frequently, the average annual return is only 11.4%, while the overall market average for the same period is 17.9%. This gap of over 6 percentage points is almost entirely caused by the transaction fees incurred with each trade. If these fees are excluded, the returns of frequent and infrequent traders end up being quite similar.
tips.benefit: This study analyzed 66,465 household accounts at US discount brokerage firms between 1991 and 1996. The group of investors who traded most often achieved an annualized return of 11.4%, while the overall market average was 17.9%, and the average return for all households was 16.4%. On average, these households turned over 75% of their stock holdings each year, swapping out three quarters of their portfolio annually. The gross returns (before transaction fees) of frequent and infrequent traders differed only slightly, meaning the performance gap is largely driven by trading costs (USA, 1991–1996).
tips.sources: Barber BM, Odean T (2000). Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth: The Common Stock Investment Performance of Individual Investors. The Journal of Finance 55(2):773-806. <https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00226>; An L, Lou D, Shi D (2022). Wealth redistribution in bubbles and crashes. Journal of Monetary Economics 126:134-153. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmoneco.2022.01.001>; Working paper draft published by the same author (October 2021, domestic figures are verified verbatim). <https://personal.lse.ac.uk/loud/AnLouShi.pdf>; Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Securities and Exchange Board of India. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: These data are from the United States in the 1990s. Indian costs differ — brokerage, securities transaction tax, stamp duty, exchange charges, GST and the bid-ask spread are charged on every trade, and the amounts were revised in recent budgets — but the core principle is the same: higher trading frequency leads to lower net returns. A trade also has to beat the spread before it earns anything. This information is not intended as investment advice.

tips.title: Do not borrow money to invest: leverage turns a fall in price into a forced sale
tips.cost: Zero if you do not borrow. If you do, the cost is the interest, which has to be beaten before any gain exists.
tips.inPlainWords: Leverage means investing with money you have borrowed. It magnifies a gain and a loss equally, and it adds a second obligation, the interest, that must be paid whatever the market does. In India you can buy shares on margin through a broker's margin trading facility, or with money borrowed on a personal loan or a credit card. In either case the lender can demand more security when the price falls and sell your holdings if you do not provide it. The sale happens at the worst moment, and a paper loss becomes a real one.
tips.benefit: The arithmetic is unforgiving: if you borrow to buy an asset and the price falls, you still owe the loan and the interest, and the broker's right to square off the position means you cannot wait for a recovery. A margin call is not a warning to ignore; it is a deadline set by someone else. The same logic makes a credit-card cash advance the worst borrowing of all, because the rate is the highest you will be offered and the compounding starts at once. If an investment is good it does not need borrowed money to be good; if it only works with leverage, the leverage is the risk.
tips.sources: Securities and Exchange Board of India. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Indian Contract Act, 1872. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: Margin trading is legal in India through a SEBI-registered broker, which makes it look safer than it is: the broker's terms, not your judgement, decide when a position is closed. Interest on a personal loan or a card advance used for investing is not deductible, so the return has to beat the rate before tax. If you already hold a leveraged position, reduce it while you can still choose the moment. This content is not investment advice.

tips.title: Using broad-market index funds instead of actively managed funds as a long-term core holding (the portion of money you keep invested for years)
tips.cost: There is no direct monetary cost. The trade-off is that you give up the chance of picking a “star fund manager.” The harder part is that when the index drops, you must endure those losses too — you can’t simply sell out midway.
tips.inPlainWords: The collection of stocks held by actively managed funds already closely mirrors the overall market. Yet the extra management fees they charge are deducted straight from your actual returns. When we repeatedly re-randomize fund performance data to test how much luck plays a role, very few funds manage to generate enough outperformance to offset those fees.
tips.benefit: Collectively, U.S. actively managed equity funds hold a portfolio very similar to the broader market. However, their high management costs directly translate into lower net returns for investors after fees are deducted. This research used a bootstrap simulation method to repeatedly shuffle fund performance data and gauge how much could be attributed to luck alone. The results show that only a tiny fraction of funds achieve excess returns large enough to cover their fees (U.S., published 2010). S&P Dow Jones Indices conducts an annual review: in 2024, 65% of U.S. actively managed large-cap equity funds underperformed the S&P 500. Over a 24-year span, an average of 64% underperformed each year. In the 15 years ending 2024, no single fund category saw a majority of active funds outperforming their respective benchmarks.
tips.sources: Fama EF, French KR (2010). Luck versus Skill in the Cross-Section of Mutual Fund Returns. The Journal of Finance 65(5):1915-1947. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2010.01598.x>; S&P Dow Jones Indices (2025). SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Year-End 2024. <https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/spiva/article/spiva-us/> (The official website refuses to be automatically captured, and the numbers are checked against the archive of 2025-05-12: <https://web.archive.org/web/20250512071051/https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/spiva/article/spiva-us/>); Harvey CR, Liu Y (2022). Luck versus Skill in the Cross Section of Mutual Fund Returns: Reexamining the Evidence. The Journal of Finance, 77(3). <https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13123> (Disputing Party); Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Securities and Exchange Board of India. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Debate exists: one study re-examined this conclusion and argued that the original Fama-French methodology of repeatedly re-sampling data might be overly strict. Under that approach, even funds with genuinely strong outperformance could be classified as “no different from luck.” Thus, the claim that “almost no active funds possess skill” might be overstated. This dataset only covers up to five years, so longer-term figures remain unavailable. This information does not constitute investment advice.

tips.title: Between two similar funds, choose the cheaper one, and buy the direct plan
tips.cost: No upfront cost to compare. The cost is the expense ratio, deducted from the scheme's assets every day, so you never receive a bill for it.
tips.inPlainWords: A fund's total expense ratio comes out of the scheme's assets, which means it reduces the return you get without ever appearing as a charge. Within the same category, the difference between a cheap fund and an expensive one is one of the few things you know in advance. In India the same scheme usually has a regular plan and a direct plan: the direct plan carries no distributor commission, so its expense ratio is lower and the gap compounds over the years you hold.
tips.benefit: The compounding is the point. On a one percentage point difference in annual cost, the ending value after twenty years is roughly 18 per cent lower for the dearer fund, and after thirty years about 26 per cent lower, assuming both earn the same before costs. Those figures come from the standard formula, not from a forecast. SEBI caps the total expense ratio a scheme may charge and requires it to be disclosed, so the number sits on the scheme's page and in its factsheet, with the direct plan's lower ratio alongside. Over a working life the difference is a year of expenses, not a rounding error.
tips.sources: Securities and Exchange Board of India. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>; SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>; Indian Contract Act, 1872. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: The comparison assumes both funds earn the same before costs; a cheaper fund that tracks its index badly can still lose. Check the exit load, the tracking error of an index fund and the portfolio, not only the ratio. A direct plan means you do the paperwork yourself; if you use a distributor you are paying for advice, which may be worth it. This information is not investment advice.

tips.title: Don’t put all your money into one stock, one platform, or one property
tips.cost: No cost at all. The hard part is accepting that you won’t always pick the single most profitable option.
tips.inPlainWords: As long as multiple assets don’t all rise or fall in perfect unison, spreading your money across them keeps your average expected returns the same, while reducing the ups and downs of your account balance. Conversely, if you invest all your funds in just one stock, platform, or property, any trouble with it directly impacts your entire portfolio.
tips.benefit: When several assets do not move in perfect lockstep, diversifying your investments maintains your expected returns while lowering overall volatility. This is the core conclusion of Markowitz’s 1952 portfolio theory, which has remained foundational for decades. On the other hand, putting all your money into one single stock or platform means its variance becomes your total portfolio variance — any rise or fall in its value directly affects your portfolio, with no other assets to offset losses when problems arise.
tips.sources: Markowitz, H. (1952). Portfolio Selection. The Journal of Finance, 7(1), 77–91. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x>; Securities and Exchange Board of India, investor education. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: This is rated as a B grade because the original academic paper relies purely on mathematical derivation, without providing concrete figures on exactly how much diversification reduces potential losses. Diversification can only lessen the fluctuations of your portfolio balance, it does not guarantee you won’t suffer any losses. Buying broad-based index funds (see item 17 in this section) is the easiest way to achieve effective diversification. This information is not intended as investment advice.

tips.title: Use the tax deduction for a pension contribution — NPS gives an extra ₹50,000 under section 80CCD(1B)
tips.cost: The NPS has a low fund-management fee, and the contribution is the money you invest. A tier-I account has a lock-in until 60, with limited partial withdrawal.
tips.inPlainWords: An individual taxpayer can claim a deduction of up to ₹50,000 a year for a contribution to the National Pension System under section 80CCD(1B) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, over and above the ₹1.5 lakh limit under section 80C. The NPS account is portable, and the corpus is taxed at maturity according to the NPS rules. The deduction is for a long-term retirement saving, not a short-term tax trick.
tips.benefit: Section 80CCD(1B) allows an additional deduction of up to ₹50,000 for an NPS contribution by an individual. The employer's contribution to NPS is deductible under section 80CCD(2) within the limits. The NPS offers a choice of active and auto allocation across equity, corporate debt, government securities and alternative assets, and the exit rules depend on the age and the corpus. The Public Provident Fund and the EPF are separate retirement vehicles with their own tax treatment.
tips.sources: Income-tax Department, deductions. <https://www.incometax.gov.in/>; Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority. <https://www.pfrda.org.in/>; National Pension System. <https://www.npscra.nsdl.co.in/>
tips.caveats: The deduction limit and the tax treatment can change with the Finance Act. An NPS tier-II account does not get the same tax treatment. Compare the NPS with the EPF and the PPF before you commit.

tips.title: Paying for gym visits individually or on short-term plans is only worthwhile if you have a consistent attendance record spanning over a year
tips.cost: Buying passes individually ends up costing more per visit compared to an annual membership. You’ll need to honestly estimate how many times per month you actually plan to go.
tips.inPlainWords: According to three years of data from U.S. gyms, members who signed contracts with monthly fees exceeding $70 attended the gym just 4.3 times per month on average, which works out to over $17 per visit. Meanwhile, a 10‑visit pass costs only $10 per visit. Collectively, these members paid roughly $600 more over their membership period. Unless you’ve already been going to the gym regularly for at least a year, buying individual passes or short‑term plans is far more economical.
tips.benefit: This study analyzed three years of data from 7,752 members at three U.S. fitness clubs. Members opting for monthly plans costing over $70 visited the gym just 4.3 times per month on average, resulting in a per‑visit cost exceeding $17. In contrast, a 10‑visit pass costs only $10 per visit. Over the same period, these members ended up paying an average of $600 more than they would have with a yearly membership. Additionally, the proportion of monthly‑plan members who kept their membership for over a year was 17% higher than that of annual‑plan members (based on three years of U.S. panel data).
tips.sources: DellaVigna S, Malmendier U (2006). Paying Not to Go to the Gym. American Economic Review 96(3):694-719. <https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.96.3.694>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: This is just one study using data from the United States. Nevertheless, its underlying principle is universally applicable: people tend to overestimate their future self‑control. If you’ve already maintained a consistent routine of going to the gym at least twice a week for a full year, then an annual membership does prove to be the cheaper option.

tips.title: Get the refund terms in writing before you pay in advance, and claim the unused balance if the business shuts down
tips.cost: No cost. The effort is refusing 'pay now, paperwork later' and reading the refund clause before you sign.
tips.inPlainWords: Gym, salon, coaching class, travel package, maintenance contract — whenever you pay for a service you will receive later, you are lending the business money. Ask for the refund, transfer and closure terms in writing, with the amount and the notice period, and keep the receipt. If the business closes, moves or stops providing the service, claim the unused balance. A refusal to refund is treated as a deficiency in service and an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
tips.benefit: India has no single statute for prepaid deposits in services such as gyms or coaching, so say that plainly: your first protection is the contract, and your second is the consumer law. A deficiency in service, and an unfair trade practice under section 2(47) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 where the trader refuses to refund, both lie, and the district commission can order a refund, compensation and costs. A card payment can also be disputed with the issuer as a chargeback, and a UPI payment through the app's dispute option. For an under-construction flat the law is stronger: the RERA Act, 2016 requires the promoter to keep most of the money in an escrow account and to refund with interest if the project fails.
tips.sources: Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016. <https://mohua.gov.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>; e-Daakhil. <https://edaakhil.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: These rights work after the money is gone, and a business that has spent it may have nothing to refund. A consumer complaint takes months and a decree still needs something to attach. So limit the float: pay per session, buy a quarter rather than a year, and never pay a large deposit for a discount you have not costed. If the business is a company in insolvency a consumer is only an operational creditor, and the recovery is slow; do not count on it.

tips.title: Wait a day before a big impulse purchase, and read the return policy before you rely on it
tips.cost: No cost beyond a day's delay. A return may cost you the shipping, and a 'free' return is often built into the price.
tips.inPlainWords: The cooling-off day is a test, not a legal right: wait 24 hours, and if you still want the thing, buy it. For online shopping, India has no general statutory seven-day no-questions-asked return. What you have is the platform's own published return policy, which the E-Commerce Rules, 2020 require it to disclose and which is enforceable as a contract, plus your rights under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 if the goods are defective, different from the description, or the refund is refused. Read the policy before you pay, not after.
tips.benefit: The saving is the impulse purchases you drop during the waiting day; there is no reliable percentage for it, which is why this is rated C. The return policy is where the money is: read the window, the exclusions (customised goods, perishables, opened digital products, innerwear, jewellery), who pays the return shipping, and whether the refund goes to the original payment method or a wallet. A refusal to refund for goods that are defective or not as described is an unfair trade practice under the Act, and an e-commerce entity must also give you its grievance officer's contact.
tips.sources: Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>; e-Daakhil. <https://edaakhil.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A 'no-questions-asked' badge is a marketing promise; the binding text is the policy page, and it can be narrower than the badge. Keep the packaging, the tags and the invoice, and photograph the parcel before you open it if the item is expensive. The cooling-off day helps only with purchases you can postpone — not with a fridge that has died or a medicine you need today.

tips.title: Don’t fall for “strikethrough prices” or impulse buying during sales
tips.cost: Zero monetary cost. The trade‑off is that you might miss out on some genuine discounts. You’ll need to keep track of the regular prices of the items you buy most often. The real challenge is resisting the urge to stock up on the day of a sale.
tips.inPlainWords: When you judge whether something is cheap, you anchor on the first price you see, and a later correction rarely undoes that impression. 'Original price 999, now 499' therefore feels like a bigger saving than it is, even when 499 is the normal price. In India the maximum retail price printed on the pack is a legal ceiling, not a bargain benchmark, and a discount measured from a price the seller never charged is a misleading representation. Track what you actually pay for the things you buy often, and treat the crossed-out figure as advertising.
tips.benefit: The anchoring effect is one of the most replicated findings in judgement research: the first number pulls the estimate, and people under-adjust. A fake reference price exploits exactly that. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 a false or misleading representation about the price or the discount is an unfair trade practice, and the consumer authority's dark-pattern guidelines single out false urgency, bait-and-switch and drip pricing. The Legal Metrology Act, 2009 makes the printed MRP the ceiling, so a 'discount' from a figure above the MRP is not a discount at all. The practical test is simple: compare the sale price with what you paid last time, not with the sticker.
tips.sources: Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Legal Metrology Act, 2009. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The anchoring research comes from laboratory studies; nobody has measured exactly how much is lost to over-buying. There are hidden costs too: stock expires, it takes space, and having it at hand makes you use more. Buy in bulk only when the shelf life is long, the need is certain and the price is genuinely below what you usually pay. Screenshot the price claim before you order, because the page can change after the sale.

tips.title: For protection, a plain risk plan is cheaper — and a savings policy's bonus is not a guaranteed benefit
tips.cost: A pure risk plan returns nothing at maturity, so the premium feels like money spent. That is the trade: you are buying cover, not a savings balance. Set aside separately the amount you would otherwise have paid into a savings policy.
tips.inPlainWords: An insurer can guarantee only what is written into the contract. In a participating, or with-profits, policy the bonus is not part of the guarantee: it is declared out of the insurer's surplus and can fall, or not be declared at all. The IRDAI (Insurance Products) Regulations, 2024 require the insurer to give you a benefit illustration that keeps the guaranteed benefits apart from the non-guaranteed ones and shows the non-guaranteed part at two assumed gross investment returns, 4% and 8%. Both are illustrations, not promises. Read the guaranteed column as the product and the non-guaranteed column as a hope, and ask what you get back if no bonus is declared at all.
tips.benefit: The distinction decides the purchase. In a non-participating savings policy the maturity benefit is fixed as an absolute amount when the policy starts; in a participating policy the bonus is not guaranteed; in a unit-linked policy the fund value follows the market. The illustration must say in writing that the non-guaranteed benefits are not guaranteed and depend on the insurer's future performance, and the 8% column is not a forecast of what you will receive. So compare products on the guaranteed column, the premium and the surrender terms, not on the larger projection. For protection alone, a term plan pays only on death and buys the largest cover for the smallest premium; the difference you keep outside the policy stays liquid and is not locked into a product that pays little if you stop early. IRDAI's rules also require the key features document and the benefit illustration to be handed to you before you sign, so ask for both and keep them.
tips.sources: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, Insurance Products Regulations, 2024. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; IRDAI, policyholder education. <https://policyholder.gov.in/>; Insurance Act, 1938. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A savings or return-of-premium policy forces a regular payment, and for someone who would not invest the difference that discipline can be worth the lower return. Whether a term plan plus your own investment beats a savings policy depends on the product and on how the money is invested, and there is no official Indian study that settles it for every case, which is why this tip carries a C grade. A bonus declared in past years is not a promise for later years, and an illustration from an earlier year may use different assumptions from today's. Surrendering early usually returns less than you paid. This is general information, not investment advice.

tips.title: Keep at least third-party motor cover: for death or injury the liability is unlimited, and only property damage is capped
tips.cost: Third-party cover is compulsory and cheap relative to the risk. A comprehensive policy adds own-damage cover and costs more. The premium rises with the vehicle's value and the add-ons, not with the third-party limit, because that limit is not a number you choose.
tips.inPlainWords: In India the compulsory motor policy is the third-party policy. Under section 147 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 the insurer must cover the insured's liability for death or bodily injury to a third party without any upper limit; only liability for damage to a third party's property is capped, at ₹7,500. So there is no small cover to top up: if your car kills or injures someone, a tribunal decides the compensation on the victim's income and age, and the insurer pays it. What you buy beyond the minimum is own-damage cover for your own car, and add-ons.
tips.benefit: Three practical points. First, drive insured: section 146 makes third-party cover compulsory, and driving uninsured is an offence. Second, the amount you are exposed to is set by a Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal under section 166, not by a policy cap — the tribunal uses the victim's income, age and dependants and the multiplier method, so an award can run into crores. Third, a comprehensive policy protects your own car and a third-party-only policy does not, so decide deliberately which one you are buying. For a hit-and-run injury the Solatium Fund can pay a fixed sum, which is a floor, not the value of the claim.
tips.sources: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. <https://morth.nic.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; Insurance Information Bureau of India. <https://iib.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The one number in the Act is the property-damage limit; do not read it as the death or injury limit. A claim can be reduced or the policy avoided if the driver had no licence, was drunk, or used the vehicle contrary to the policy — and the insurer may pay the victim and then recover the money from you. Third-party premium is regulated, so shop on the insurer's service and claim record rather than on a 'bigger' limit. Verify the current text of the Act and the policy wording before you buy, because the Act has been amended more than once.

tips.title: Set aside an emergency fund equal to 3–6 months of living expenses in a readily accessible account
tips.cost: There is no direct monetary cost. The trade-off is forgoing higher returns; the funds must be kept in a checking account, money market fund, or any deposit account that allows immediate withdrawals. The real challenge lies in resisting the urge to dip into the fund while saving it up.
tips.inPlainWords: Keep 3 to 6 months’ worth of living expenses in an account you can withdraw from at any time. This way, if you lose your job or fall ill, you won’t have to borrow money at an 18% annual interest rate, nor will you need to sell your investments at a loss.
tips.benefit: An emergency fund eliminates the need to borrow money or sell investments at a loss during unexpected events like job loss or illness. For details on the minimum annual interest rates for consumer loans and credit card payments, see Section 7 of this chapter (which advises against relying on minimum credit card payments).
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India, financial literacy. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Securities and Exchange Board of India, investor education. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The recommendation to save 3–6 months’ worth of expenses is a widely accepted guideline, but no official or academic sources have been identified to support it, hence the C grade. The required amount should be calculated based on your regular monthly expenses, not your income. This information does not constitute investment advice.

tips.title: Run a quick comparison before paying off your mortgage — don’t rely on gut feeling
tips.cost: No cost at all. It only takes about half an hour to do the math. You’ll need to honestly estimate the steady after‑tax return you can expect over the long run.
tips.inPlainWords: Paying off your mortgage is essentially the same as earning a guaranteed return equal to your mortgage rate. So the only question you need to ask is: can you reliably earn a higher after‑tax return than that rate? If the answer is yes, it makes sense to keep the money invested. If not, or if you’re unsure, paying off the loan is the better choice. With an equal principal‑and‑interest repayment plan, most of the early payments go toward interest; the earlier you pay, the more you save. Most bank apps have a “pre‑payment calculator” that gives you the exact numbers.
tips.benefit: The calculation works like this: let r be the annual mortgage rate as stated in your contract. Next, let g represent the after‑tax annual return you can expect from an alternative investment — the average percentage gain you’d earn each year by putting that money elsewhere. Paying off the mortgage guarantees you a return of exactly r; each dollar you apply to the loan earns you that rate for sure. If g consistently exceeds r, it’s better to keep the money invested. If g is lower than r, or if you can’t reliably predict it, paying off the loan locks in a risk‑free return equal to r. Again, because most of the early payments under an equal principal‑and‑interest plan cover interest, the earlier you pay, the more you save.
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India, home loans. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; National Housing Bank. <https://nhb.org.in/>
tips.caveats: This section provides only the calculation method, not a definitive recommendation. It’s relatively rare for investment returns to reliably surpass mortgage rates. Regardless of which option you choose, be sure to keep enough cash on hand for emergencies. Also, check your contract for any prepayment penalties. This information is not intended as financial advice.

tips.title: Judge an online seller by the invoice, the seller's details and the platform's record, not by followers or five-star reviews
tips.cost: No cost. Ten minutes to read the seller's page, the return policy and the platform's grievance contact before you order.
tips.inPlainWords: The parts of an e-commerce listing you can check are the ones that matter: who the seller is, where they are, the MRP, the return and refund policy, and a grievance officer with a contact. Reviews are the weakest signal, because they can be bought; India now has a national standard for online consumer reviews, and the consumer authority's dark-pattern guidelines bar interfaces that manufacture false urgency or hide a charge. If a seller takes your money and does not deliver what was described, the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 gives you a refund and compensation, and the marketplace can be liable where it fails its duties under the e-commerce rules.
tips.benefit: The consumer commission can order a refund, replacement or compensation for a defective product or a deficient service, and a misleading representation about a product is an unfair trade practice. The e-commerce rules require the marketplace to disclose the seller's identity and contact and to run a grievance mechanism, which is why a written complaint to the platform is both the first step and the record you will need later. The dark-pattern guidelines let the consumer authority act against a platform that adds a charge at checkout without consent or makes cancellation deliberately hard. None of this requires proving a criminal cheat.
tips.sources: Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bureau of Indian Standards. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A five-star average over a hundred reviews is cheap to manufacture; read the one-star reviews and the return policy instead. A countdown timer and a pre-ticked add-on are dark patterns, and a screenshot of them is evidence. An advance you pay is governed by the contract, and a forfeiture clause that works as a penalty can be challenged; if the seller defaults, claim the advance back. India has no statutory rule that triples the price for every fraud, so the realistic award is the refund, the loss and the cost of the complaint.

tips.title: If something goes wrong after buying from a livestream, first ask the platform for the seller’s and influencer’s details — they’re required to provide them.
tips.cost: No cost involved; you simply need to request the information from the platform.
tips.inPlainWords: One of the biggest hurdles when problems arise from purchases made during livestreams is figuring out exactly who to hold responsible. In such cases, you can demand that the platform disclose the identity of the livestream operator and any associated influencers, along with their business records. The platform is legally obligated to comply with this request.
tips.benefit: When consumer disputes occur, operators of livestream marketing platforms must furnish buyers with the relevant details of both the livestream operator and any affiliated influencers, as well as all related business documentation. The primary obstacle in pursuing legal recourse in these situations is identifying the right party to sue; obtaining this information removes that barrier entirely.
tips.sources: Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: Before making any purchase, be sure to record both the livestream footage and any promises made by the host. Should any issues arise, first request the seller’s and influencer’s information from the platform before deciding whether to file a complaint or pursue legal action. This same regulation also outlines three additional requirements: first, merchants cannot unilaterally expand the list of items excluded from the seven-day no-questions-asked return policy; second, such exclusions must never be set as default options; and third, merchants are prohibited from denying returns without your explicit consent.

tips.title: If food is unsafe, you can claim compensation — the FSS Act and the consumer law apply
tips.cost: A consumer complaint has a small fee; the FSSAI complaint is free. A lab test may cost money; the FSSAI can arrange one.
tips.inPlainWords: If you buy food that is unsafe, adulterated or mislabelled, you can complain to the FSSAI or the local food safety officer, and claim a refund and compensation under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The FSS Act, 2006 also provides for penalties and compensation. Keep the bill, the packaging and the sample. India does not have a single 'ten times the price' rule for every case; the compensation depends on the loss and the forum.
tips.benefit: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 allows a consumer to complain to the food safety officer and the adjudicating officer, and provides for compensation for injury. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 allows a complaint before the district, state or national commission, and the court can award compensation for a defect. The FSSAI can test the sample and prosecute the manufacturer. A hospital record and the bill are the evidence.
tips.sources: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A 'best before' date is not a guarantee of safety after opening. A claim for a large amount needs medical evidence. Do not throw away the packaging or the remaining food before you complain.

tips.title: Check the ISI mark, the BEE star label and the label on the box before you buy a big appliance
tips.cost: No cost. A few minutes on the BIS and BEE websites, or in the BIS Care app, before you order.
tips.inPlainWords: Three marks carry most of the information. The ISI mark means the product is certified by the Bureau of Indian Standards against the Indian Standard for that product, and the licence number on the label can be checked. The BEE star label gives the energy-efficiency rating and the annual electricity consumption, so a higher star rating means a smaller bill. The packaged-commodity label gives the maximum retail price, the net quantity, the month and year of manufacture, and the manufacturer's details. Together they tell you whether the product may legally be sold and what it will cost to run.
tips.benefit: The Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 makes certification compulsory for the products on the BIS list and penalises a false or misused ISI mark; the BIS Care app lets you enter the licence number or the HUID and see whether it is real. The star label is issued under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001 for the appliances the Bureau of Energy Efficiency has scheduled, and it carries the annual energy consumption in units — the number that repeats on your electricity bill. The Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 require the MRP, quantity, date and consumer-care details to be printed, and an e-commerce listing must show them too.
tips.sources: Bureau of Indian Standards. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; Bureau of Energy Efficiency. <https://beeindia.gov.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The ISI mark certifies conformity to a standard; it is not a ranking, and it does not mean the product is better than a certified rival. The star rating is measured under test conditions, so your bill depends on how you use the appliance. A seller who shows a certificate image, or a licence number that does not match the model on the box, is worth avoiding — check the number yourself. The lists of products that need certification and star labels change, so check the current list rather than a blog post.

tips.title: Treat jewellery, watches and collectibles as spending, not as savings: the tax and the making charge are gone on day one
tips.cost: The cost is the purchase: GST, customs duty on an imported watch, and the making charge on jewellery. None of it returns when you sell.
tips.inPlainWords: A large part of what you pay for a watch, a piece of jewellery or a collectible is not the asset. On gold jewellery you pay GST and a making charge for design and labour; on an imported watch you pay customs duty and GST; on a collectible you pay whatever the seller can get. On resale the buyer pays for the metal or the model, not for the making charge or the tax, and the gap is a loss before any question of appreciation. If you love the object, buy it as spending; do not stretch the budget because you expect it to be worth more later.
tips.benefit: The distinction a dealer will not draw for you: investment gold is bullion or a coin sold by weight with a small premium, while jewellery is sold by design with a making charge that can be a large part of the price. A BIS hallmark tells you the purity and the HUID can be verified, but neither says what you will be offered on resale. Pre-owned luxury watches do trade, and that market prices the model, the box and the papers, not the story. Collectibles have no floor at all. The honest comparison is with the same money invested, not with a hoped-for resale price.
tips.sources: Bureau of Indian Standards, hallmarking. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs. <https://www.cbic.gov.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: If you pawn an item, the lender values the metal or a conservative estimate, not the price you paid, and the interest runs from the day you take the loan; pawnbroking is governed by the state's pawnbrokers law and by the contract, so read the forfeiture and auction clauses before you sign. A jeweller's buy-back promise usually means exchange against another purchase and often excludes the making charge. Gold bought to hedge against inflation should be bullion or a gold fund, not a necklace. This is not investment advice.

tips.title: For gold, check the BIS hallmark and the six-digit HUID; for gemstones, insist on a report from an accredited laboratory
tips.cost: No cost to check a hallmark. A gemstone or jewellery report from a laboratory costs money, and the seller usually pays for the one it shows you.
tips.inPlainWords: A printed certificate proves nothing by itself; what matters is who issued it and whether you can verify it. In India gold jewellery sold above the statutory purity threshold must carry a BIS hallmark: the purity grade (22K, 18K), the assaying centre's mark and a six-digit HUID that you can check in the BIS Care app. Hallmarking covers the metal, not the stone. A gemstone report is only as good as the laboratory, so look for one accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories, and read what the report actually says — 'treated', 'synthetic' or 'dyed' in the description is the price difference.
tips.benefit: The BIS hallmarking scheme turns a claim about purity into something you can verify in the shop, and the HUID is unique to the piece. For a stone, the report matters when it states the species, the treatment and the weight, and when the laboratory is accredited for that test; a report that only says 'certified' or 'A-grade' tells you nothing, and 'A-grade', 'old mine' and 'unprocessed' are sales words, not Indian standards. The invoice is part of the protection: it must describe the article, the purity and the weight, because that description is what a consumer commission will compare the goods against.
tips.sources: Bureau of Indian Standards, hallmarking. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A hallmark certifies the metal's purity and nothing else; it does not value the piece and says nothing about the stone. Certificates and HUID labels can be copied, so check the number in the app while you are in the shop rather than trusting a photograph. A laboratory report is an opinion at a point in time, and a stone can be treated after it was tested. Buy from a licensed jeweller, get a full invoice, and pay by card or UPI so a record exists. A claim that a stone cures a disease is false advertising under the consumer law.

tips.title: Treat a blind box or a gacha draw as money that will not come back — India has no odds-disclosure law, so check before you pay
tips.cost: No fee to look, and no legal minimum spend. Set a hard budget before the first draw and keep it on a separate card or wallet limit. The cost that matters is the total over a month, not the price of one box.
tips.inPlainWords: A blind box, a loot box or a gacha pull sells you a chance at an item, and the seller decides what is inside. India has no statute that compels a blind-box or gacha seller to publish the odds, the stock of a limited item, or a minimum-purchase guarantee, so you cannot rely on a disclosure right of the kind some other markets give a buyer. What Indian law does give you is a set of general levers. A misleading claim about what you might win is an unfair trade practice and a misleading advertisement under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The consumer authority's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns catch an interface that manufactures false urgency, hides a charge or tricks you into a purchase. The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 prohibits online money games outright. So read whatever odds the platform does publish, and treat an in-app purchase as final unless the platform's own refund policy says otherwise.
tips.benefit: Five levers, in the order you would use them. First, the platform's own published rules: where it states odds, a pity timer for a guaranteed item or a rule for converting duplicates, that statement is a representation you can hold it to, and a screenshot is evidence. Second, the Consumer Protection Act, 2019: a false or misleading representation about a product, its price or what a purchase includes is an unfair trade practice, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority can act against a misleading advertisement. Third, the CCPA's Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023, which name the interface tricks a gacha screen relies on — false urgency, drip pricing, basket sneaking and disguised advertising — and give the authority a route against a platform that uses them. Fourth, the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, which require an intermediary, including an app store or a platform carrying the promotion, to make reasonable efforts to stop users posting content that encourages gambling or is contrary to law, which is the hook for an advertisement that dresses a paid draw up as a game. Fifth, the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025: if the draw takes a stake and pays a cash prize, it is a prohibited online money game and the problem is no longer a consumer complaint.
tips.sources: Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Central Consumer Protection Authority, Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023. <https://ccpa.gov.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, IT Rules, 2021. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: None of this makes the sale void or entitles you to your money back because you did not get the item you wanted; what you can challenge is a false statement, a hidden charge or a prohibited game, not bad luck. Keep the published rules, the odds screen and the unboxing on record before you complain, because the page can change after the sale. A minor's purchase is the strongest case, as section 9 of this chapter explains, and a parent who funded the wallet knowingly has a weaker one. The dark-pattern guidelines are enforced by the consumer authority against a platform rather than by you as a claim in a forum, so use them to frame a complaint. If the draw takes a stake and offers a cash prize, stop paying: since the 2025 Act that is an online money game and it is banned.

tips.title: Packaged food carries a legal label; loose food carries less information, so ask
tips.cost: No cost. Read the label and compare the per-100 g values, not the front-of-pack claim.
tips.inPlainWords: A packaged food product must carry the FSSAI licence number, the ingredient list, the net quantity, the nutritional information, the date marking and the veg or non-veg mark. A loose product sold from a bin is not required to carry the full label, so you cannot compare it in the same way. If you care about additives and allergens, buy a packaged product with a readable label or ask the seller for the source.
tips.benefit: The FSSAI Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020 require the mandatory declarations on a packaged food label, and the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 add the MRP and quantity. A loose product must still be safe and not misbranded, but the full nutritional panel is not required. The FSSAI can act on a mislabelled or unsafe product. A packaged product with a damaged or missing label is a risk.
tips.sources: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, labelling. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs, Legal Metrology. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A 'no added sugar' claim does not mean no sugar. A 'natural' claim is not a nutritional claim. A loose product with no date is a freshness risk.

tips.title: Stocks that have lost value should also be sold according to pre‑set rules — don’t try to even out costs by buying more
tips.cost: No cost at all. The hard part is admitting the loss and actually selling the stock.
tips.inPlainWords: Human nature drives us to sell winners and hold losers. In seven years of data from 10,000 U.S. accounts, stocks that rose were sold about 50% more often than those that fell. The same investors also tended to add to positions in losing stocks. Yet over the following year those unloved losers underperformed the sold winners by an average of 3.4 percentage points.
tips.benefit: This study examined every trade made by 10,000 accounts at a U.S. discount broker from 1987 to 1993. The proportion of profitable stocks sold (PGR) was 0.148, while the proportion of losing stocks sold (PLR) was 0.098 — a difference of 0.050 with a t‑value exceeding 35. In other words, rising stocks were sold more than 50% more often than falling ones. Investors also bought losing stocks more frequently: the re‑purchase rate for losers was 0.135 versus 0.094 for winners, again with a strong statistical significance. The data also contradicted the belief that “stuck stocks will eventually bounce back.” Over the next year, the excess returns of sold profitable stocks exceeded those of kept losing stocks by 3.4 percentage points. These excess returns represent performance above the market index. As a concrete illustration, selling $1,000 worth of a losing stock instead of a winning one would yield roughly 4.4% more return in the following year; this figure includes tax savings from the early sale under U.S. tax rules (1987‑1993).
tips.sources: Odean T (1998). Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses? The Journal of Finance 53(5):1775-1798. <https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00072>; Securities and Exchange Board of India, investor education. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: This point addresses the decision “to sell or not to sell”; point 15 (“avoid excessive trading”) deals with how often to trade — the two are not contradictory. Following a pre‑defined rule actually reduces the number of trades. Mathematically, buying more shares does lower the average cost per share, but treating this as a way to recover losses is misguided; it merely increases the amount of capital tied up in a single stock (see point 19, “don’t bet everything on one stock”). The data originate from U.S. accounts in the 1980s‑1990s; trading costs and tax regimes differ for A‑share investors. This information is not intended as investment advice.

tips.title: Investing abroad? Use the RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme through your bank, or a fund based in India — not an unregulated app
tips.cost: A bank charges a margin over the market rate, a remittance fee and GST on the fee; a fund based in India charges its expense ratio. Either is small next to the cost of an unauthorised route.
tips.inPlainWords: A resident individual may invest in foreign shares and funds through the RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme, which allows a capped remittance each financial year for permitted purposes, including investment in foreign securities, through an authorised-dealer bank. So the legal route is your own bank's remittance service with the correct purpose, or an Indian mutual fund or exchange-traded fund that invests abroad and is bought in rupees. Money sent through a friend's account, an unregulated app or a hawala channel is a foreign-exchange violation, and it leaves you with no enforceable claim if the platform disappears.
tips.benefit: The scheme gives you a documented, auditable route: the bank checks the purpose, the remittance is in your own name, and the holding is yours. An India-domiciled international fund or ETF gives you the same exposure without a remittance, and the fund handles the foreign-currency paperwork; the trade-off is a limited menu and the industry-wide overseas investment limit, which has from time to time forced funds to stop taking fresh money. Either way the investing principles in items 17 and 19 apply: a broad index, no concentration in one market, and a horizon long enough to survive a bad decade.
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India, Liberalised Remittance Scheme. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Securities and Exchange Board of India. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>; Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Income Tax Department. <https://www.incometax.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Read the scheme's current rules before you remit: the annual cap (USD 250,000 per person per financial year at the time of writing), the permitted purposes and the declaration change with each budget, and a purpose code that does not match the use is your problem, not the bank's. A remittance for a purpose the bank does not recognise can be refused or reversed.
