An overseas broker may not be regulated in India, so a dispute has no Indian forum; check that the platform is one your bank will remit to. Past returns in a foreign market tell you nothing about the next ten years. This is information, not investment advice.

tips.title: Insure only the losses your savings cannot absorb; use an emergency fund for the small ones
tips.cost: A premium is a real cost; compare the cover, the waiting period and the exclusions, not only the price. An emergency fund earns a modest interest.
tips.inPlainWords: Insurance is for a loss that would wreck your finances, not for every small expense. Buy health cover, term life cover if someone depends on your income, and motor third-party cover because the law requires it. Pay small repairs, a broken phone or a routine dental bill from an emergency fund. A policy with a low deductible and a high premium can cost more than the risk it covers.
tips.benefit: A health insurance policy and a term life policy transfer a catastrophic risk to the insurer. The IRDAI regulates the products and the claim process, and a policyholder has a grievance route. The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 requires at least third-party cover. An emergency fund of three to six months of expenses in a liquid account covers the small shocks and reduces the temptation to borrow.
tips.sources: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; Policyholders' education. <https://policyholder.gov.in/>; Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, financial literacy. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>
tips.caveats: A policy excludes pre-existing conditions for a waiting period. A low premium can mean a high deductible or a narrow network. Do not cancel a health policy to save a small premium.

tips.title: If someone at home depends on your income, buy term life insurance for the breadwinner first — not for your kids.
tips.cost: A few hundred to a few hundred rupees per year, depending on age, coverage amount, and policy length (this is a rough estimate by the author; no official figures exist). Be sure to disclose your health status truthfully before applying; the process takes about half an hour.
tips.inPlainWords: Term life insurance covers you only for a set number of years. If you die during that period, your family receives the sum assured. The cover is meant to protect people who rely on your earnings — an unpaid home loan, children still in school. If nobody depends on your income, term cover is not a priority. A child earns nothing, so a policy on a child replaces no income; insurers set their own caps on child policies, and a child policy is usually a savings product with an insurance wrapper.
tips.benefit: The Indian rulebook is thin on amounts and firm on definitions. Term insurance pays only on death within the term; whole life runs for the lifetime; an accident policy pays only for accidental death or disability and is not a substitute for life cover. A policy on someone else's life needs that person's consent and an insurable interest, and a proposal that conceals a material fact can be repudiated within the period the Insurance Act, 1938 allows. IRDAI does not prescribe a sum assured: the insurer's underwriting and your income decide what you can buy, so the useful starting point is the outstanding loans plus the household expenses until the children are independent, checked against what the insurer will actually issue.
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Securities and Exchange Board of India. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The C rating reflects the absence of official Indian guidance on the right amount, not doubt about the priority: a child's death does not remove household income, while the earner's death leaves the loan instalments and the school fees behind. When money is tight, insure the adults first — term life and a one-year health policy — before considering a child policy. Read the exclusion list and the claim-settlement record before you choose an insurer, and disclose your health history truthfully, because a claim can be refused for a non-disclosure. See Section 7, item 20 on one-year medical cover.

tips.title: Changed your mind about a policy? You have a 30-day free-look window, and cancelling costs the risk premium, not the whole premium
tips.cost: No fee to cancel. The refund is the premium less the risk premium for the days you were covered and any medical-examination cost the insurer paid — not the whole amount, and not a flat charge.
tips.inPlainWords: Every life and health policy in India carries a free-look period: 30 days from the day you receive the policy document, under the IRDAI's policyholder-protection rules. Read the policy inside that window. If it is not what you were sold, write to the insurer and cancel; you get the premium back minus the proportionate risk premium for the days of cover and the medical-test cost. After the window you get the surrender value the product provides, which for a traditional policy is usually available only after you have paid two full years of premium, and is often well below what you paid.
tips.benefit: The free-look right is the cheapest exit you will ever have from a policy you do not want, and it exists precisely because insurance is sold rather than bought. The insurer must print the free-look terms in the policy, and the refund basis is prescribed, so you can check the arithmetic. It matters most for a savings or endowment policy sold as an investment, and for a unit-linked plan where the early charges are heavy: the difference between cancelling inside the window and surrendering three years later can be most of what you paid. If the policy was mis-sold — a different product, a false promise of returns — the free-look complaint is also the cleanest record of the dispute.
tips.sources: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; IRDAI policyholder education. <https://policyholder.gov.in/>; Insurance Act, 1938. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: The window runs from receipt of the document, not from the sale, so note the date the policy was delivered. It is a right to reconsider, not a right to a full refund: the risk premium for the days on cover and the medical-examination cost are deducted. After the window a late surrender can lose a large part of the premiums, and a unit-linked policy's fund value can be below the premiums paid. Do not cancel health cover you need before the replacement policy is issued and its waiting periods have started, and do not cancel a policy you are claiming under.

tips.title: At a bank counter, ask one question before you sign: is this a deposit or an insurance policy?
tips.cost: No cost. Read the product name on the form and ask for the benefit illustration and the free-look clause before you sign anything.
tips.inPlainWords: A bank branch that sells you insurance is acting as a corporate agent for an insurer; it is not taking a deposit. The IRDAI (Registration of Corporate Agents) Regulations and IRDAI's policyholder-protection rules require the seller to identify the insurer, hand you the policy documents and the benefit illustration, and not pass the product off as a bank deposit or a bank-guaranteed saving. Two documents settle the question. A deposit appears on your statement as a deposit, the bank owes it back, and it carries deposit insurance. A policy is a contract with an insurer, the bank owes you nothing on it, and leaving it early usually costs money. If the paper names an insurer and a sum assured, it is insurance.
tips.benefit: The Indian rules here are about disclosure rather than a prescribed wording on the cover. A corporate agent must be registered with IRDAI and must disclose the insurer it represents; it must not describe an insurance product as a deposit or as a bank product, and it must not present an uncertain return as guaranteed. The policyholder-protection regulations give you a free-look period of 30 days from receipt of the policy document, during which you can cancel and get the premium back less the proportionate risk premium for the days on cover and the medical-examination cost. Make the comparison honest: a bank deposit is a debt the bank must repay and is covered by deposit insurance up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank under the deposit-insurance scheme, while an insurance policy pays only on the events and terms written into it and its surrender value in the early years can be well below the premiums paid. If you were told the policy was a deposit or a fixed return, that is mis-selling, and the route runs from the insurer's grievance officer to IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal and then to the Insurance Ombudsman.
tips.sources: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, Registration of Corporate Agents Regulations. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; IRDAI, Bima Bharosa grievance redressal. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; Insurance Ombudsman. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, deposit insurance. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Insurance Act, 1938. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A bank employee who earns a commission on the policy is not a neutral adviser; ask whether the person is paid for the sale. The free-look clock runs from the day you receive the policy document, not the day you signed, so write that date down. A 'guaranteed' return in a brochure is guaranteed only if it is written into the contract as an absolute amount, which is how a non-participating product works; a participating policy's bonus is not. Elderly relatives are the usual target, so check what they signed while the free-look period is still open. If the bank will not give you the policy document, complain to the insurer and to IRDAI, because the document is what starts your rights. This is general information, not financial advice.

tips.title: Cancel or complain about a policy through the insurer, then Bima Bharosa and the Insurance Ombudsman — never through a 'refund agent'
tips.cost: No cost. The insurer's grievance officer, the IRDAI portal and the Insurance Ombudsman do not charge you; the effort is in writing the complaint down.
tips.inPlainWords: Advertisements that promise a 'full refund of your policy' or a 'hundred per cent surrender' are selling a service you can do yourself for nothing. They take a share of whatever comes back, ask for your policy, PAN, Aadhaar, bank details and OTPs, and sometimes coach you to sign a false complaint that the policy was mis-sold. The result is the same surrender you could have made, at a lower payout, with your data in someone else's hands. If you were misled, write to the insurer's grievance redressal officer first; if that does not settle it, escalate to IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal and then to the Insurance Ombudsman.
tips.benefit: The Indian route is free and time-bound. Every insurer must publish a grievance redressal officer and a complaint procedure, and the policyholder-protection rules set a deadline for a reply. If the reply does not come, or does not satisfy you, the IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal records the complaint against the insurer, and the Insurance Ombudsman, set up under the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017, hears the dispute at no cost, can order the insurer to pay, and its award binds the insurer. A consumer commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 remains open for a deficiency in service. None of these routes needs an intermediary.
tips.sources: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, Bima Bharosa. <https://bimabharosa.irdai.gov.in/>; IRDAI. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; IRDAI policyholder education. <https://policyholder.gov.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: Surrender is final: the cover stops that day, and a new policy at an older age, or after a diagnosis, can cost more or be refused. If the premium is the problem, ask the insurer about a reduced paid-up policy or a policy loan before you surrender — both keep some cover alive. The Ombudsman's award binds the insurer only if you accept it; you can still go to a consumer commission or a court. And never sign a complaint that describes a sale that did not happen: a false allegation is your liability, not the agent's.

tips.title: Name a nominee on every policy, and keep a register your family can find — the claim clock is shorter than you think
tips.cost: No cost. A nomination is a form at purchase, and a change needs a written request to the insurer.
tips.inPlainWords: If no nominee is named, the money is paid to the legal heirs and waits for succession, which is slow and often ends in a family dispute. Under section 39 of the Insurance Act, 1938 you name a nominee, and the insurer is discharged by paying that person. What the nominee then does with the money is the part people get wrong: the Act distinguishes a beneficiary nominee from a collector nominee, and the courts have differed on whether the nominee keeps the money or holds it for the heirs. So name the right person, and if you want the money to reach one particular person, make a will as well. Tell your family which insurers you are with.
tips.benefit: The nomination is what lets a family claim without a succession certificate, and it is the cheapest estate-planning step there is. The claims clock in India is not five years: a civil claim on a policy is governed by the Limitation Act, 1963, which gives three years from the date the right to sue accrues, and a consumer complaint must be filed within two years of the cause of action under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Separately, section 45 of the Insurance Act stops an insurer from questioning a life policy on the ground of misstatement after three years, so an old policy is hard to repudiate except for proved fraud. Both facts reward a family that acts promptly and keeps the papers.
tips.sources: Insurance Act, 1938. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; Limitation Act, 1963. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A nomination is not a will: it tells the insurer whom to pay, and heirs can still challenge it. Update it after a marriage, a divorce, a birth or a death — an old nomination in favour of an ex-spouse is a dispute waiting to happen. Keep one list of the policies, the policy numbers and the insurers, and tell one reliable person where it is; a policy nobody knows about is money the family never claims. For a claim, the death certificate, the policy document and the nominee's KYC are the basic papers. A claim rejected for a missing document can usually be revived; one barred by limitation usually cannot.

tips.title: Do not speculate in crypto: it is not legal tender in India, the tax is punitive, and a collapsed platform is hard to sue
tips.cost: Zero if you stay out. If you are already in, the cost of getting out is the spread and the tax on any gain.
tips.inPlainWords: Crypto tokens are not legal tender in India and are not a currency. The RBI has warned against them and the tax law treats them as virtual digital assets: a gain is taxed at a flat rate, the set-off of losses is denied, and tax is deducted at source on each transfer, so frequent trading is expensive even when you break even. Holding is not illegal, but the protections you get with a bank deposit or a mutual fund — a regulated intermediary, a compensation route, a statement you can rely on — do not exist here. If a platform freezes withdrawals, your remedy is a civil suit against a company that may have nothing left.
tips.benefit: The reason to stay out is not a forecast that the price will fall; it is that the downside is asymmetric in a way you cannot hedge. A winning trade is taxed and a losing one cannot be set off, so a churn of small gains can leave a bill larger than the profit. The market is also where the frauds collect: fake apps, signal groups, guaranteed-return schemes and wallet-draining approvals. India now requires virtual-asset service providers to register as reporting entities under the anti-money-laundering law, which helps at the margin, but it is not deposit insurance.
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Income Tax Department. <https://www.incometax.gov.in/>; Cyber Crime Portal, Ministry of Home Affairs. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>; Department of Economic Affairs. <https://dea.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Never let anyone route money through your bank account to buy crypto; that is a money-laundering exposure for you, not a favour. Do not connect a wallet to a link you did not expect, and revoke approvals you do not recognise. If you are defrauded, report at cybercrime.gov.in or on 1930 at once, because the trail is traced in hours, not weeks. If you hold tokens, keep the records the return needs — exchange statements, wallet addresses and dates — because the burden of proof is yours. A fall in price is not a recoverable loss, and a platform that has spent the money is a poor defendant.

tips.title: Self-employed? Build a pension with NPS, PPF or EPF — there is no single 'minimum bracket' trick
tips.cost: The NPS charges a fund-management fee; the PPF has a low interest rate but no market risk. The contribution is the main cost.
tips.inPlainWords: A self-employed person has no employer pension. The main routes are the National Pension System, the Public Provident Fund and, for a covered establishment, the EPF. The NPS gives a tax deduction under section 80CCD(1B), the PPF is a safe long-term saving, and the EPF is available only through an eligible employer. Start early and contribute regularly; a last-minute contribution buys less pension.
tips.benefit: The NPS, the PPF and the EPF have different contribution, lock-in, return and tax rules. The PFRDA regulates the NPS, and the PPF is a government-backed small-saving scheme. A self-employed person can open an NPS tier-I account and choose the allocation; the PPF has a 15-year term that can be extended. The EPF requires an establishment covered by the EPF Act. The right mix depends on age, risk and liquidity.
tips.sources: Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority. <https://www.pfrda.org.in/>; National Pension System. <https://www.npscra.nsdl.co.in/>; National Savings Institute, PPF. <https://www.nsiindia.gov.in/>; Employees' Provident Fund Organisation. <https://www.epfo.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The tax rules and the contribution limits change. An NPS annuity is taxable in part. Do not put all your retirement money in one product. Check the PFRDA and the PPF rules.

tips.title: Inspect a new vehicle before delivery and keep the invoice, warranty and RTO papers
tips.cost: No cost to inspect. A professional PDI costs a small fee and can reveal a repaired vehicle.
tips.inPlainWords: Before you take delivery, inspect the paint, the tyres, the odometer, the lights and the spare wheel, and check that the VIN matches the invoice. Keep the invoice, the warranty booklet, the insurance and the registration papers. A defect in the first months is a warranty claim; a major defect can be a consumer complaint. Do not accept a vehicle with a repaired panel or a mismatched VIN.
tips.benefit: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers a manufacturing defect and a deficient service. The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and the Central Motor Vehicles Rules require a valid registration and insurance. The warranty is a contract term, and a refusal to honour it can be a consumer complaint. A pre-delivery inspection (PDI) report signed by the dealer is evidence. The RTO registration and the VIN should match.
tips.sources: Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. <https://morth.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A 'zero kilometre' claim can be false; check the odometer and the manufacturing date. Do not sign the delivery note before the inspection. A used car needs a different check.

tips.title: Buying a used car? Check the RC, the hypothecation and the challans before you pay, and put the 'no major accident, no flood' promise in the contract
tips.cost: A pre-purchase inspection by a workshop costs a few thousand rupees; the VAHAN and challan checks are free. Budget an hour for the paperwork and a day for the transfer.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no public accident-history database a buyer can search, so the paperwork and an inspection are your evidence. Check the registration certificate on the VAHAN portal or the mParivahan app, confirm there is no hypothecation or blacklist entry and no pending challan, and match the chassis and engine numbers. Ask the dealer to write into the invoice and the sale agreement that the car has had no structural accident repair, no flood damage and no fire damage. If that promise is false the dealer has misrepresented the quality of the goods, which is an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
tips.benefit: The consumer commission can order the dealer to take the car back, refund the price and pay compensation, and the Act's product-liability provisions allow damages for a defect. India does not have a statutory 'triple damages' rule, so do not expect a multiple of the price: the realistic recovery is the price, the repair or inspection costs and compensation for the loss, which is why the written promise and the inspection matter more than the threat of litigation. Section 50 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 requires the transfer to be applied for within fourteen days, so complete it instead of driving on the seller's registration certificate.
tips.sources: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, VAHAN. <https://vahan.parivahan.gov.in/>; Parivahan Sewa. <https://parivahan.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: The consumer route is strongest against a dealer; in a private sale you are in contract law, so inspect before you pay and do not rely on assurances. An 'as is' clause does not protect a seller who actively conceals damage, but proving concealment takes documents and an expert. Ask the insurer about the claim history and the no-claim bonus, and remember that a cheap car with a pending loan, a duplicate registration certificate or an expired fitness certificate is a problem you inherit. Pay by bank transfer so a trail exists.

tips.title: At a car dealership, refuse unauthorised 'financial service' fees and check every line of the invoice
tips.cost: No cost to ask. A loan from your bank may be cheaper than the dealer's offer.
tips.inPlainWords: A car dealer may charge for the vehicle, GST, registration, insurance and an optional accessory, but it cannot add an undisclosed 'financial service' fee or force you to buy insurance or a loan from it. Ask for a written break-up before you pay, and compare the loan terms with your bank. A forced add-on can be an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
tips.benefit: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 prohibits an unfair trade practice and a restrictive trade practice. The RBI's fair-practice rules apply to a loan, and the IRDAI rules apply to insurance; a lender or insurer cannot be forced on you. The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 requires the registration and the third-party insurance. A written quotation and the invoice are the evidence. A dealer cannot retain the registration certificate for an add-on.
tips.sources: Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, fair practices. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. <https://morth.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A genuine service fee should be disclosed and agreed. A 'discount' can hide a higher interest rate. Do not sign a blank delivery note or a loan form.

tips.title: Taken to shops that were not in your tour contract? Claim from the Indian tour operator, not the shop
tips.cost: No cost to complain. Keep the contract, the itinerary, the invoices, the card slips and the goods unused; a complaint and mediation can take a few months.
tips.inPlainWords: A package tour is a service, and the operator you paid in India is the party you can pursue even when the shop is abroad. If the itinerary you signed did not include shopping stops, or the operator added them, the tour you received is not the tour you bought. Write to the operator, set out what was promised and what happened, and ask for a refund of the purchases you were pushed into and of any activity you paid for and did not get. India has no designated-shopping-store rule and no statutory thirty-day return, so your claim rests on the contract and on the consumer law.
tips.benefit: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 a deficient service and a misleading representation about the tour are both actionable, and the district commission can order a refund, compensation and costs. The Ministry of Tourism's approval and classification scheme for tour operators gives you a second lever: a complaint to the Ministry or the state tourism department about an approved operator can put its approval at risk. The Ministry's 24x7 tourist helpline (1363) can point you to the right office, and the National Consumer Helpline can help you file. A card payment can also be disputed with the issuer, though the window is short.
tips.sources: Ministry of Tourism. <https://tourism.gov.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: If the itinerary you signed listed the shopping stop, or you signed a consent form on the bus, your case weakens; argue the price and the misrepresentation instead. The overseas shop is outside Indian jurisdiction, so pursue the operator, not the shop. Complain in writing while the tour is fresh — receipts, the guide's name and the itinerary's wording fade, and a consumer complaint has a two-year limit from the cause of action. The cheapest tours are priced on the assumption of kickbacks; a tour that costs less than the flights is worth a second look before you pay.
